column1: What is the fundamental gear ratio equation relating angular velocity to tooth count?
column2: R = ω_out / ω_in = N_driver / N_driven — output speed ratio equals the inverse ratio of tooth counts.

column1: Alternative gear ratio formula used for torque/mechanical advantage analysis — how is R defined in terms of driven/driver teeth?
column2: R = N_driven / N_driver. When R > 1, output rotates slower with more torque (reduction); when R < 1, output spins faster with less torque (overdrive).

column1: If an 8-tooth driver gear meshes with a 24-tooth driven gear, what is the speed and torque relationship at the output?
column2: The output (24-tooth) rotates at 1/3 the input speed but delivers 3x the torque — tooth counts set an inverse speed/torque tradeoff.

column1: Why must tooth pitch be constant across two meshing gears?
column2: Because the driver and driven gear must advance by the same arc length (same number of teeth) at the mesh point; constant pitch ensures correct kinematic constraint and clean meshing.

column1: What geometric tooth profile do LEGO gears use, and what property does it guarantee?
column2: An involute tooth profile, derived from unwrapping a string from a base circle; it guarantees constant velocity ratio transmission and minimizes sliding friction, even with minor center-distance variation.

column1: What is the 'line of action' in gear meshing?
column2: The straight line along the pressure angle (typically 20° in LEGO gears) where tooth flanks contact and all useful torque transfer occurs.

column1: Name the five core LEGO Technic gear types and their primary spatial function.
column2: Spur gears (parallel shafts), bevel gears (perpendicular intersecting axes), worm gears (perpendicular non-intersecting axes, high reduction + self-locking), double-bevel gears, and crown gears (flat disk, right-angle coupling to multiple pinions).

column1: What unique mechanical property do worm gears provide that spur/bevel gears do not?
column2: Self-locking behavior — they provide massive speed reduction and resist backdriving, allowing them to hold a load without the output rotating back into the input.

column1: How is the overall ratio of a multi-stage (compound) gear train calculated?
column2: It equals the product of all individual stage ratios (e.g., a 3:1 stage followed by a 5:1 stage yields 15:1 overall), enabling extreme ratios without impractical single gear sizes.

column1: What is the role of an idler gear in a gear train, and does it affect the overall ratio?
column2: An idler gear repositions drive shafts spatially or controls rotational direction/phase without contributing to the overall gear ratio — it cancels out in the ratio calculation.

column1: What is the typical per-stage efficiency range for LEGO spur gear meshes, and what causes the losses?
column2: Approximately 85–95% (some sources cite 70% for worm gears under heavy load); losses come from sliding friction at tooth flanks, rolling resistance at bearings, and axle-to-bushing friction.

column1: What is the fundamental power/torque tradeoff invariant in any gearbox, regardless of material (Lego, metal, etc.)?
column2: Power continuity via conservation of energy: P = τ·ω must be conserved (minus friction losses) across every stage — you can trade torque for speed or vice versa, but never gain both simultaneously from a fixed power source.
